claims.evidence: This describes the software used for decoding analysis.

claims.claim: The behavioral impact of the distractor types was tested using a paired t-test.
claims.source: The behavioral impact of the distractor types was tested using a paired t-test, comparing accuracies and reaction times.
claims.evidence: This describes the statistical test used for behavioral data.

claims.claim: One-tailed testing was performed for behavioral comparisons given the hypothesis that the strong distractor would be detrimental to performance.
claims.source: Given the hypothesis that the strong distractor would be detrimental to performance, one-tailed testing was performed.
claims.evidence: This describes the directionality of the statistical test based on the hypothesis.

claims.claim: Randomly shuffled trial labels were generated 500 times to create a null distribution for informative activity.
claims.source: In order to make the source projected classifier weights ('informative activity') more interpretable, we generated randomly shuffled trial labels and re-ran the same classifier and source projection approach. This was done 500 times, and the empirically observed values at each time and grid point were z-transformed using the mean and standard-deviation from the randomized data.
claims.evidence: This describes the permutation procedure for statistical testing of informative activity.

claims.claim: A nonparametric cluster permutation approach was employed to control for multiple comparisons, normally using 5000 randomizations.
claims.source: To control for multiple comparisons, we employed a nonparametric cluster permutation approach as proposed by Maris and Oostenveld, 2007 normally using 5000 randomizations.
claims.evidence: This describes the multiple comparison correction method used.

claims.claim: Power modulations were operationalized using a log10([high power] / [low power]) ratio.
claims.source: To this end, power modulations were operationalized using a log10([high power] / [low power]) ratio and correlated with the respective difference in the strength of memorized information.
claims.evidence: This describes the quantification method for power modulation.

claims.claim: Modulations of oscillations in the alpha to beta range in task-relevant sensory regions have been suggested to play an important role for functional inhibition or prioritization.
claims.source: Modulations of oscillations in the alpha to beta range in task-relevant sensory regions have been suggested to play an important role for both mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about existing theoretical frameworks in the field.

claims.claim: Regionally specific power changes around the alpha frequency range have been linked to top-down-mediated gain modulation, with enhanced power reflecting relatively inhibited states.
claims.source: In particular, regionally specific power changes around the alpha frequency range have been linked to such a putative top-down-mediated gain modulation, with enhanced power reflecting relatively inhibited states (Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Klimesch et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This cites theoretical frameworks about the functional role of alpha oscillations.

claims.claim: Increased alpha power in parieto-occipital cortical regions contralateral to the unattended hemifield is a very robust finding in the visual modality.
claims.source: For example, increased alpha power in parieto-occipital cortical regions contralateral to the unattended hemifield is a very robust finding (e.g. Busch and VanRullen, 2010; Thut et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This cites empirical evidence from the visual attention literature.

claims.claim: The general inhibitory gating function of localized alpha increases has been reported with respect to more specific visual features, leading to spatially circumscribed alpha modulations.
claims.source: The general inhibitory gating function of localized alpha increases has also been reported with respect to more specific visual features, leading to remarkable spatially circumscribed alpha modulations (Jokisch and Jensen, 2007; Zumer et al., 2014) even at a retinotopic level (Popov et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This cites evidence for feature-specific alpha modulations in vision.

claims.claim: Alpha increases have been reported during the retention period in the visual, somatosensory and auditory modalities, putatively protecting the to-be-remembered information against interference.
claims.source: Also for the domain of working memory, alpha increases have been reported during the retention period in the visual (e.g. Jensen et al., 2002; Klimesch et al., 1999), somatosensory (e.g. Haegens et al., 2009) and auditory modalities (e.g. Obleser et al., 2012), putatively protecting the to-be-remembered information against interference.
claims.evidence: This cites evidence for alpha increases in working memory across modalities.

claims.claim: Circumscribed decreases in alpha to beta power (desynchronization) have been deemed functionally important in the context of working-memory tasks.
claims.source: This load-dependent top-down amplification of alpha and its concomitant inhibition account are widely accepted, but circumscribed decreases in alpha to beta power (often labeled as desynchronization) have also been deemed functionally important in the context of working-memory tasks.
claims.evidence: This describes an alternative theoretical perspective on alpha/beta power changes.

claims.claim: In a prioritization account, alpha/beta desynchronization reflects an enhanced activation of performance-relevant neural ensembles.
claims.source: In a prioritization account, they reflect an enhanced activation of performance-relevant neural ensembles (e.g. Noh et al., 2014; Sauseng et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This describes the prioritization account of alpha/beta desynchronization.

claims.claim: A framework by Hanslmayr et al., 2016 explicitly links the extent of alpha/beta desynchronization to the representational strength of the information content in episodic memory.
claims.source: A recent framework by Hanslmayr et al., 2016 explicitly links the extent of alpha/beta desynchronization to the representational strength of the information content in episodic memory (for supportive evidence see Griffiths et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This cites a theoretical framework linking desynchronization to memory strength.

claims.claim: A framework by van Ede, 2018 stresses the importance of regionally specific alpha and beta decreases when item-specific information needs to be prioritized in the retention period of working-memory tasks.
claims.source: This is in line with a framework by van Ede, 2018 stressing the importance of regionally specific alpha and beta decreases when item-specific information needs to be prioritized in the retention period of working-memory tasks.
claims.evidence: This cites a theoretical framework on prioritization in working memory.

claims.claim: Temporal cues can be exploited such that when distracting sound input can be temporally predicted, inhibition or prioritization processes should be regulated in an anticipatory manner in relevant auditory regions.
claims.source: Besides stimulus-feature information, which can influence the precise location of alpha modulations in the visual system (Popov et al., 2019), temporal cues can also be exploited (Rohenkohl and Nobre, 2011; van Ede and Chekroud, 2018): that is, when distracting sound input can be temporally predicted, inhibition or prioritization processes should be regulated in an anticipatory manner in relevant auditory regions.
claims.evidence: This describes the theoretical prediction about temporal anticipation of distractors.

claims.claim: An increasing amount of evidence points to a functional role of alpha oscillations in listening tasks.
claims.source: As in other sensory modalities (Frey et al., 2015; Weisz and Obleser, 2014), an increasing amount of evidence points to a functional role of alpha oscillations in listening tasks.
claims.evidence: This summarizes the state of evidence for alpha in auditory tasks.

claims.claim: Increased alpha oscillations have been observed in putatively visual brain regions when focusing attention on auditory input in cue-target periods.
claims.source: Increased alpha oscillations have been observed in putatively visual brain regions when focusing attention on auditory input in cue-target periods (Frey et al., 2014; Fu et al., 2001; Snyder and Foxe, 2010).
claims.evidence: This cites evidence for cross-modal alpha modulation during auditory attention.

claims.claim: A similar posterior alpha pattern is observed in challenging listening situations, for example, with increased cognitive load or when faced with background noise.
claims.source: A similar posterior pattern is also observed in challenging listening situations, for example, with increased cognitive load or when faced with background noise (for reviews see Johnsrude and Rodd, 2016; Rönnberg et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This cites evidence for alpha modulation in challenging listening conditions.

claims.claim: Increases in alpha oscillations as a mechanism for selective inhibition have rarely been shown for auditory cortex.
claims.source: However, increases in alpha oscillations as a mechanism for selective inhibition (Strauß et al., 2014) have rarely been shown for auditory cortex, in which feature-specific processing of target and distractor sounds takes place.
claims.evidence: This characterizes the state of evidence for alpha increases in auditory cortex.

claims.claim: Different lines of evidence show an association between (also illusory) sound perception and low auditory cortical alpha power.
claims.source: With regards to alpha desynchronization in auditory cortex, different lines of evidence showing an association between (also illusory) sound perception and low auditory cortical alpha power (e.g. Lange et al., 2014; Weisz et al., 2007; Weisz and Obleser, 2014; for invasive recordings illustrating sound-sensitive alpha desynchronization in anterolateral Heschl's Gyrus, see Billig et al., 2019), suggest a link to representational content as described above.
claims.evidence: This cites evidence linking low alpha power to sound perception in auditory cortex.

results.result: The study employed 33 healthy participants in a modified auditory Sternberg task with strong and weak distractors presented in a counterbalanced blockwise design during a 2-second retention period.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 provide comprehensive methodological details about the experimental design, including participant count, task structure, distractor types, and timing. Claims C119-C124 document appropriate participant screening, ethical approval, and exclusion criteria. The experimental design is clearly described and adequately controlled.

results.result: Strong distractors produced a small but statistically significant decrease in accuracy (85% vs 83%, p=0.02, Cohen's d=0.37) compared to weak distractors, while reaction time differences were not significant.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10 report the behavioral data with appropriate statistical tests and effect sizes. The one-tailed test (C8) is justified by the directional hypothesis. The small effect size and non-significant RT difference are appropriately acknowledged (C11-C12), supporting the conclusion that strong distractors were slightly more challenging.

results.result: Linear discriminant analysis with 5-fold cross-validation successfully decoded whether probes were part of the memory set, with above-chance performance beginning ~334 ms post-probe (p=4e-4, Cohen's d>0.8) and lasting until 700 ms.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C16 provide detailed methodological and statistical information about the decoding analysis. The timing (C14-C15), effect sizes (C16), and cross-validation procedure (C159) are clearly reported. The interpretation regarding early sensory activation (C17-C18) is appropriately cautious and supported by citations.

results.result: Time-generalized decoding revealed reduced strength of memorized information prior to strong distractors, with significant differences at ~200 ms pre-distractor (p=0.0156) and below-chance decoding for strong distractors (t32=-3.98, p=3.63e-04).
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C20 establish the methodological rationale for time-generalized decoding as a proxy for memory strength. Claims C31-C38 report the temporal dynamics and statistical results, including the below-chance decoding phenomenon. The interpretation (C36) is supported by the data, though the below-chance decoding requires careful interpretation (addressed in C39-C41).

results.result: Source localization using beamformer-projected classifier weights identified widespread informative activity with left-hemispheric dominance, most prominently in left superior temporal gyrus (lSTG).
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C27 describe the source localization results, while C161-C165 provide detailed methodological information. The approach is adapted from established methods (Marti & Dehaene, 2017) and includes appropriate statistical controls (permutation testing, z-scoring). The identification of lSTG as the primary region is data-driven and well-justified.

results.result: Left superior temporal gyrus was selected as the region of interest for spectral analysis based on its established role in speech processing and phonological short-term memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C29 appropriately cite previous literature to justify the functional role of lSTG. Claim C30 logically follows from the source localization results (C27) and the cited literature, making this a reasonable methodological decision.

results.result: Induced alpha/beta power in lSTG decreased prior to strong distractors compared to weak distractors, with significant differences (p=0.0104) at peak frequencies of ~12-13 Hz and ~21-22 Hz.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 report the spectral analysis results with appropriate statistical testing. The finding of alpha/beta power decrease (C46, C83) is clearly documented and statistically significant (C47). The comparison to the visual modality study (C49) provides important context, though it reveals an opposite pattern.

results.result: No significant pre-distractor evoked alpha power or phase alignment was observed, contrasting with findings in the visual modality.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C53 report the negative finding regarding evoked alpha with multiple analytical approaches (time-frequency analysis, ITC). The statistical test (C53) confirms no significant difference. Claims C54, C88-C89 appropriately contextualize this negative finding within the broader literature.

results.result: Trials sorted by pre-distractor beta power showed that low beta power was associated with relatively increased strength of memorized information (t32=2.27, p=0.03), while alpha power bins showed no significant difference (t32=0.06, p=0.95).
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C56 describe the power-binning methodology. Claims C59-C62 report the ANOVA results showing a significant interaction and frequency-specific effects. The interpretation (C63) that beta desynchronization supports prioritization is appropriately cautious and supported by the statistical results.

results.result: Individual differences in alpha power modulation were negatively correlated with differences in memory strength (r=-0.36, p=0.04), driven by high-power trials, while beta showed no such correlation (r=0.06, p=0.72).
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C67 report the correlation analyses with appropriate statistics. The differential pattern between alpha and beta (C65-C66) is clearly documented. The interpretation (C68-C70) that alpha and beta have distinct functional roles is supported by the data, though the mechanisms remain to be fully elucidated.

results.result: Frequency-resolved decoding revealed that memory-related information is primarily carried by theta band activity (1-7 Hz), not alpha/beta, with temporal fine structure containing additional information beyond amplitude modulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73 address the potential circularity concern by showing alpha/beta bands do not carry decodable memory information. Claims C74-C78 demonstrate that theta band activity is superior for decoding. The interpretation (C79-C81) that alpha/beta modulations enable rather than carry information is well-supported and addresses an important mechanistic question.

results.result: Below-chance decoding prior to strong distractors reflects a systematic relative absence of memory-item specific patterns, though some representation must be present, potentially in activity-silent form.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40 appropriately contextualize the below-chance decoding phenomenon with citations. However, the interpretation (C41) and speculation about activity-silent processes (C42-C43) remain tentative. While the reasoning is logical, the precise neural mechanisms underlying below-chance decoding are acknowledged as challenging to pinpoint (C40).

results.result: The current findings of alpha/beta power decreases prior to strong distractors contrast with alpha/beta increases observed in the analogous visual modality study, suggesting modality-specific differences in oscillatory mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C89 document the discrepancy between the current auditory findings and previous visual modality results. The comparison is appropriate and well-cited. The speculation about modality-specificity (C90-C91) is reasonable but acknowledged as uncertain, appropriately suggesting this as a topic for future investigation.

results.result: Alpha and beta oscillations in auditory cortex show functionally distinct contributions to memory prioritization, with beta desynchronization accompanying prioritization generally and alpha effects being more level-dependent.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93 synthesize the main findings regarding differential alpha/beta roles, appropriately citing theoretical frameworks. Claims C113-C115 provide the specific interpretation of these differences. Claim C94 adds supporting evidence about modulation extent. The conclusion (C95) about methodological value is appropriate.

results.result: The study demonstrates a direct relationship between alpha/beta power in auditory cortex and strength of memorized information, supporting the view that desynchronization enables rather than carries memory content, which is primarily represented in theta activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C104 appropriately position the study's contribution. Claims C105-C106 connect findings to theoretical frameworks with appropriate citations. Claims C107-C108 specify the frequency content of memory representations. Claims C111-C112 provide the summary conclusions, which are well-supported by the collective evidence.

results.result: The MEG experiment employed standard preparation procedures, appropriate stimulus delivery systems with measured timing compensation, and a counterbalanced block design with 12 blocks of 24 trials each.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C143 provide comprehensive methodological details about MEG preparation, stimulus delivery, timing compensation, and experimental structure. The procedures are standard and appropriate. The timing compensation (C134-C135) is particularly important for accurate temporal analysis.

results.result: MEG data were acquired at 1 kHz and preprocessed using signal space separation, filtering, epoching, ICA-based artifact removal, resulting in no trial rejections and final data rank of 45-48.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C158 provide detailed preprocessing pipeline information. The methods are standard and appropriate for MEG analysis. The use of signal space separation (C148-C149), ICA with PCA preprocessing (C153-C155), and the resulting data quality (C157-C158) are well-documented. The extensive preprocessing justifying no trial rejection (C158) is reasonable.

results.result: Spectral and statistical analyses employed appropriate methods including Fourier transform with frequency-adaptive windows, nonparametric cluster permutation testing with 5000 randomizations, and permutation-based normalization of source-projected classifier weights.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C175 document the analytical methods with appropriate detail. The spectral analysis approach (C166-C168), software tools (C169-C170), statistical testing (C171-C174), and power modulation quantification (C175) are all standard and appropriate for the research questions. The use of established toolboxes (Fieldtrip, MVPA-Light) enhances reproducibility.

results.result: The findings support a prioritization account of auditory working memory protection, though future studies using neuromodulation and more naturalistic stimuli are needed to establish causality and generalizability.
results.evaluation: Claim C44 appropriately connects decoding and behavioral results. Claims C109-C110 provide theoretical reconciliation with previous literature. Claims C116-C118 appropriately acknowledge limitations and suggest future directions, including the need for causal manipulation (C117) and testing generalizability to natural speech (C118).

results.result: Previous literature on alpha oscillations in auditory tasks has primarily focused on non-auditory regions, selective attention paradigms, or working memory without predictable distractors, with indirect associations to auditory information processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C102 provide appropriate literature review contextualizing the current study. The characterization of previous work is accurate and well-cited. This establishes the novelty of the current approach in directly linking auditory cortical alpha/beta to memory strength with predictable distractors.

results.result: Theoretical frameworks propose that alpha/beta oscillations in sensory regions mediate both inhibition (via power increases) and prioritization (via desynchronization), with extensive evidence in visual modality but limited direct evidence in auditory cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C176-C190 provide comprehensive theoretical background with appropriate citations. The review covers both inhibition and prioritization accounts (C176-C184), temporal prediction (C185), and modality-specific evidence (C186-C190). This establishes the theoretical motivation for the study and highlights the gap in auditory cortex research.
